title: Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts

concept.text: The innovation would be a broadly transferable framework for predicting how real surfaces touch, deform, stick and separate, starting from measured surface topography and independently characterized bulk and interfacial properties. Its outputs would include actual contact area, contact stiffness, adhesion and loading–unloading hysteresis—the difference between the loading and unloading responses associated with energy dissipation. The intended advance is reliable prediction across materially different contact conditions without repeatedly fitting the model to each experiment.

Real surfaces meet through roughness at multiple scales. Their response can combine elastic recovery, permanent plastic deformation, time-dependent viscoelastic deformation and adhesive forces. Surface shape also changes with loading and sliding, so predicting an evolving contact requires accounting for the geometry produced by its mechanical history. Existing idealized theories and specialized numerical methods address important portions of this problem; the proposed capability would connect these portions more reliably.

Scope synthesis: the goal is a transferable predictive framework with explicit applicability limits. It does not require one closed-form equation for every material pair and environment. Evolution of contact geometry through deformation belongs within this concept; prediction of accumulated wear, damage and component lifetime is assigned separately to MEC-11.

significance.text: The potentially revolutionary step would be making coupled interface response predictable from independently measured inputs across a substantially wider range of surfaces and materials. Contact area, stiffness, adhesion and hysteresis would be direct outputs of that capability. Müser and Nicola describe an existing foundation of theoretical and computational tools that produce realistic predictions from material properties and topography; the proposed innovation would extend their transferability and treatment of interacting mechanisms.

Conditional application synthesis: better contact predictions could reduce extensive prototyping and improve design decisions for seals, tires, grippers, implants and precision contacts. The supplied review connects contact mechanics to interface compliance, adhesion, dissipation and seal leakage, providing a technical basis for such possibilities. Product-level improvements would still depend on application-specific validation and additional governing physics; successful prediction of an interface response would not by itself establish the performance of a complete device.

Impact synthesis: a benchmark spanning two carefully chosen material pairs would be a meaningful step toward this capability, but would not establish transfer across all the named applications. The impact claim depends on subsequent demonstrations across additional materials, geometries and operating histories. Nor would better contact mechanics alone establish reliable lifetime wear prediction.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is robust prediction when roughness, adhesion and nonlinear or history-dependent deformation materially interact. In their publication-era assessment, Müser and Nicola identified successful modeling of linearly elastic, nonadhesive bodies, while systematic extensions beyond topographies satisfying the random-phase approximation remained scarce. This is a specific limitation on the surface descriptions covered systematically, rather than evidence that rough-contact mechanics as a whole lacked predictive methods.

A concrete coupled challenge is adhesive hysteresis when viscoelasticity and roughness-induced multistability both contribute substantially. Viscoelasticity makes deformation depend on time and loading history; multistability allows the rough interface to occupy different mechanical configurations and switch between them. Predicting either contribution separately does not establish that their combined dissipation is reproduced. The review's authors reported that they were unaware of studies successfully reproducing this combined behavior at publication.

Other concrete barriers include rigorous treatment of plasticity and coupled viscoelasticity–adhesion, and accounting for surface topography that changes during loading and sliding. A transferable model must use the evolving geometry to predict subsequent contact response, rather than treating the initial surface as permanently fixed. The supplied review documents these difficulties historically; it does not establish which remain unresolved in November 2026.

current_state.text: Multiscale methods already model important rough-contact problems. Martin H. Müser and Lucia Nicola's review, “Modeling the surface topography dependence of friction, adhesion, and contact compliance,” appeared in MRS Bulletin volume 47, associated with 2022, and was published online on 18 January 2023. It describes substantial success for linearly elastic, nonadhesive contacts and an increasing number of tools producing realistic predictions from material properties and surface topography.

That progress had a defined scope. The authors described systematic extensions beyond random-phase topographies as scarce and rigorous treatments of nonlinear and nonlocal behavior—including plasticity and coupled viscoelasticity–adhesion—as relatively recent. Their stated lack of awareness of successful reproduction of jointly substantial viscoelastic and multistability-driven adhesive hysteresis is a dated assessment, not proof that no subsequent result exists.

The supplied validation reports that the retained HTML contains the complete article text and that the PDF spans all eight article pages, with neither extraction truncated. Figures were not visually inspected, and this account relies on the reported textual findings rather than values inferred from plots. Although the source index records retrieval on 11 November 2026, retrieval does not update the article's scientific assessment. No freshness-search results were supplied to establish how the identified limitations changed by the review's 1 November 2026 cutoff.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: use measured initial surface topography and independently characterized bulk and interfacial properties to make blind predictions of contact area, stiffness, adhesion and loading–unloading hysteresis. Test both a rough viscoelastic material pair and a rough elastic–plastic pair over multiple loads and rates. Include conditions where adhesion and dissipative mechanisms materially affect the response, so a nominally broad benchmark cannot succeed only in easier limiting cases.
completion_criteria.label: Blind contact-response predictions across rough viscoelastic and elastic–plastic pairs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evolution and transfer tests: measure deformation-induced topography changes during repeated loading and unloading, and test whether the model predicts both those changes and their consequences for subsequent contact response. Evaluate a new geometry without refitting the predictive model. These tests would connect the demonstration to evolving contacts and distinguish transfer from fitting individual experiments.
completion_criteria.label: Predict topography evolution and transfer contact predictions without refitting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and acceptance criteria: pre-register error tolerances, uncertainty criteria, operating ranges and the rules governing any calibration. Include independent experiments, report failures alongside successes, and make sufficient measurement and model information available for replication. No numerical acceptance thresholds are supplied here; they would need to be justified for the intended uses. These are proposed evaluation choices, not established standards prescribed by the source.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-register acceptance criteria and report independently reproducible results, including failures

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation boundary: passing this program would demonstrate useful breadth within the tested materials, geometries, loads, rates and histories. Finite tests cannot establish literal universality, complete device performance or lifetime wear prediction. Broader claims would require further independent demonstrations and explicit boundaries on applicability.
completion_criteria.label: State applicability boundaries supported by the tested contact conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based scope synthesis: MEC-11, “Transferable prediction of wear and component life,” is the closest adjacent concept. MEC-12 concerns how surfaces touch and respond mechanically, including deformation-induced changes in topography; MEC-11 concerns accumulated wear and lifetime. They interact because changing topography alters contact response, while contact stresses and dissipation can matter to wear. Only MEC-11's title and the supplied scope assignment are available, so its detailed boundary cannot be verified.

Roster-based comparison: MEC-02, “Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts,” concerns achieving and sustaining an exceptionally low-friction operating condition. MEC-12 concerns predicting contact response across broader regimes, including adhesive and dissipative ones. Better contact mechanics could inform analysis of low-friction interfaces, but demonstrating predictive mechanics would not establish durable superlubricity, and demonstrating superlubricity would not establish broad predictive transfer.

Roster-based comparison: MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” and MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” address material performance. Their properties could affect the deformation of contacting bodies, but fatigue immunity and high bulk strength are distinct from predicting a rough interface. MEC-13, “General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms,” could potentially use contact predictions when designing mechanisms with interacting surfaces; synthesis of mechanisms remains a separate capability. These comparisons are based on roster titles rather than full records for those concepts.

change_log.change: Preserved MEC-12's identity while explaining the framework's inputs, outputs and treatment of evolving topography.
change_log.reason: The concept concerns transferable prediction of contact response; consolidation needed to retain its physical detail and distinguish it from lifetime wear prediction.

change_log.change: Removed temperature coupling from the evidence-backed list of contact mechanisms.
change_log.reason: The supplied review's discussion of heat transport through contacts does not substantiate coupled temperature-dependent contact mechanics. This narrows the supported claim without asserting that thermal coupling is unimportant.

change_log.change: Dated the technical assessment and distinguished 2026 source retrieval from scientific freshness.
change_log.reason: The supplied source supports a publication-era account, while the empty freshness-search record cannot establish the remaining gaps as of November 2026.

change_log.change: Specified the successful linearly elastic, nonadhesive regime and retained the limitations involving random-phase topographies and coupled hysteresis.
change_log.reason: These scientific distinctions explain both existing achievements and the concrete difficulty of extending them.

change_log.change: Separated direct predictive outputs from conditional benefits to complete products.
change_log.reason: The source supports the technical basis for interface prediction; benefits across seals, tires, grippers, implants and precision contacts remain application-dependent extrapolations.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed benchmark to include interfacial properties, substantial coupled dissipation, evolving topography, independent experiments and geometry transfer.
change_log.reason: These refinements test the difficult mechanisms and evolving-contact identity while preserving their status as proposed criteria.

change_log.change: Preserved source-access limitations and qualified related-concept comparisons.
change_log.reason: The supplied review reports complete text extraction but no visual inspection of figures, and neighboring concepts are represented only by roster titles and limited scope notes.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish which publication-era limitations persisted or were resolved by November 2026.
The record does not establish whether later work reproduced adhesive hysteresis with both substantial viscoelasticity and roughness-induced multistability.
Numerical error tolerances, uncertainty requirements, material pairs, operating ranges and practical computational limits for the proposed benchmark remain unspecified.
Temperature-dependent contact mechanics is not substantiated by the supplied evidence; its eventual place within the framework remains open.
The precise division between deformation-driven topography evolution in MEC-12 and wear-driven evolution in MEC-11 requires the full MEC-11 record.
Passing the proposed two-pair benchmark would leave broader material transfer and the named product-level benefits to be demonstrated.
